letters.name: a
letters.memoryTrick: Like the 'a' in English 'father' or 'cat' — a short, open sound. Think of saying 'ah' at the doctor.

letters.name: bé
letters.memoryTrick: Same as English 'b' — press your lips together and release. Like the 'b' in 'baby' or 'balloon'.

letters.name: cé
letters.memoryTrick: Two faces: hard like 'k' in 'cat' before a/o/u, soft like 's' in 'cent' before e/i/y. The cé rule is like the English 'c' in 'city' vs 'cat'.

letters.name: dé
letters.memoryTrick: Same as English 'd' — tongue taps behind your upper teeth. Think of the 'd' in 'door' or 'dance'.

letters.name: e
letters.memoryTrick: The French 'e' has several faces: a neutral schwa like the 'u' in English 'upon', or open like 'e' in 'bed'. At the end of a word it is usually silent!

letters.name: effe
letters.memoryTrick: Same as English 'f' — top teeth on lower lip and blow air. Like the 'f' in 'flower' or 'friend'.

letters.name: gé
letters.memoryTrick: Two faces, like 'c': hard 'g' as in 'go' before a/o/u, soft 'zh' as in 'mirage' before e/i/y. Just like English 'g' in 'giraffe' vs 'goat'.

letters.name: ache
letters.memoryTrick: The French 'h' is silent — always! It's a ghost letter. But it still matters: a 'mute h' allows liaison, an 'aspirated h' blocks it.

letters.name: i
letters.memoryTrick: Like the 'ee' in English 'see' or 'meet' — a clean, tense vowel said with the tongue high and forward. Think 'eee' with a smile!

letters.name: ji
letters.memoryTrick: Like the 's' in English 'pleasure' or 'measure' — a soft 'zh' sound. Think of Zsa Zsa Gabor's first initial!

letters.name: ka
letters.memoryTrick: Same as English 'k' — a crisp, unvoiced click from the back of the throat. Rare in native French words; mostly appears in borrowings.

letters.name: elle
letters.memoryTrick: Similar to English 'l' but lighter — tip of the tongue touches behind the upper teeth, not curled back. Think of a delicate 'la la la'.

letters.name: emme
letters.memoryTrick: Same as English 'm' — lips together, hum through your nose. Like the 'm' in 'mama' or 'moon'.

letters.name: enne
letters.memoryTrick: Same as English 'n' — tongue tip behind your upper teeth, air through the nose. Like the 'n' in 'noon' or 'nice'.

letters.name: o
letters.memoryTrick: Either closed like 'oh!' (lips rounded tight) or open like 'aw' in English 'bought'. The closed 'o' sounds like the English letter name 'O'.

letters.name: pé
letters.memoryTrick: Same as English 'p' — a crisp pop of the lips. However, in French it has no puff of air after it; it's a drier, less explosive 'p' than in English.

letters.name: qu
letters.memoryTrick: In French, 'q' is almost always followed by 'u' and sounds like 'k'. Think of 'qu' as a team — like the 'c' in English 'cat'.

letters.name: erre
letters.memoryTrick: The famous French guttural R — produced at the back of the throat, almost like gently gargling. Not rolled on the tongue like Spanish or Italian!

letters.name: esse
letters.memoryTrick: Like 's' in English 'sun' when at the start or doubled. Between vowels it becomes 'z' like in 'rose'. Think of it as a snake that sometimes buzzes like a bee!

letters.name: té
letters.memoryTrick: Like English 't' but without the puff of air — a clean tap behind the upper teeth. Think of saying 'tea' but keeping it crisp and dry.

letters.name: u
letters.memoryTrick: The tricky French 'u' — round your lips as if to say 'oo' but say 'ee' instead. It's a sound English doesn't have! Practice: purse lips tightly and try 'eee'.

letters.name: vé
letters.memoryTrick: Same as English 'v' — top teeth on lower lip, voice buzzing. Like the 'v' in 'voice' or 'victory'.

letters.name: double vé
letters.memoryTrick: Rare in French — mostly in borrowed words. Pronounced like English 'w' or sometimes like French 'v'. The letter is called 'double vé' — literally 'double v'!

letters.name: ixe
letters.memoryTrick: Usually sounds like 'ks' (as in English 'box'), but between vowels it can be 'gz' (as in 'exact'). At the end of words like 'deux' it's silent!

letters.name: i grec
letters.memoryTrick: Called 'Greek i' — acts like a regular 'i' (ee sound) when alone, or like a 'y' glide (as in English 'yes') between vowels. Think 'i grec = Greek i'.

letters.name: zède
letters.memoryTrick: Like the 'z' in English 'zebra' or 'buzz' — a voiced buzz with the tongue near the roof of the mouth. Don't say 'zee', say 'zed'!

letters.name: a accent grave
letters.memoryTrick: Sounds just like regular 'a' — the accent grave only distinguishes meaning (à = 'to/at' vs a = 'has'). It's a spelling mark, not a sound change!

letters.name: a accent circonflexe
letters.memoryTrick: A slightly deeper, more open 'ah' sound — like the 'a' in English 'father'. The circumflex often marks where an old 's' used to be (hôpital → hospital).

letters.name: a tréma
letters.memoryTrick: Extremely rare in French — the tréma tells you to pronounce this 'a' separately from the vowel before it. Sounds just like regular 'a'.

letters.name: e accent aigu
letters.memoryTrick: The sharp, bright 'ay' sound — like the first part of the English letter 'A' but without the glide. Think 'eh' but with a smile, tense and forward.

letters.name: e accent grave
letters.memoryTrick: An open 'eh' sound — like the 'e' in English 'bed' or 'let'. More relaxed and open than é. Think of saying 'meh' with your mouth slightly more open.

letters.name: e accent circonflexe
letters.memoryTrick: Sounds like è (open 'eh' as in 'bed'). The circumflex often marks a vanished 's' — tête was once 'teste', forêt was 'forest'.

letters.name: e tréma
letters.memoryTrick: The tréma means 'pronounce me separately!' It breaks up a vowel pair — in Noël, you say 'No-el', not 'nohl'. Sounds like è.

letters.name: i accent circonflexe
letters.memoryTrick: Sounds just like regular 'i' (ee as in 'see') — the circumflex on î does not change the sound, it only marks a lost 's' from older spelling.

letters.name: i tréma
letters.memoryTrick: The tréma on ï says 'I'm my own syllable!' In 'maïs' it's 'ma-ees', not 'may'. Helps keep vowels from blending together.

letters.name: o accent circonflexe
letters.memoryTrick: A closed, rounded 'oh' sound — tighter than plain 'o'. Think of the English 'oh!' but with lips more pursed and tense.

letters.name: u accent grave
letters.memoryTrick: Used in only one French word: 'où' (where). The accent distinguishes it from 'ou' (or). Sounds just like regular French 'u'.

letters.name: u accent circonflexe
letters.memoryTrick: Sounds the same as regular French 'u'. The circumflex marks a lost 's' — 'coûter' once had an 's' just like English 'cost'.

letters.name: u tréma
letters.memoryTrick: Very rare in French. The tréma keeps 'u' pronounced separately from a preceding vowel. In modern spelling, often replaced with 'üe'.

letters.name: y tréma
letters.memoryTrick: Extremely rare — appears only in a handful of proper names and archaic spellings. Sounds like regular 'i'. You may never encounter it outside a dictionary!

letters.name: e dans l'o
letters.memoryTrick: A true French specialty — 'œ' is a single fused letter. In 'œuf' it sounds like 'uh' (rounded), in 'œufs' like a tight 'eu'. It's 'e' melted into 'o'!

letters.name: e dans l'a
letters.memoryTrick: A rare Latin-import ligature in French — 'a' and 'e' fused together. Sounds like 'é' (ay). Mostly seen in Latin expressions like 'ex æquo'.
